title: He wept over the city (Luke 19:41–48)
hook: coming near Jerusalem, he weeps: if only you knew the things of peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, cloaks on the road, Zechariah's king on a colt, and Jesus saying that if the crowd were silent, the stones would shout. Your line was the stones would cry out. What good thing did you say out loud? Day five hundred seventy-one.

Coming down the Mount of Olives today, the road bends, and suddenly the whole of Jerusalem is laid out across the valley: walls, domes, towers, the old city glowing gold in the late light. People stop and take photos. Luke says that when Jesus came to that point, in the middle of the singing crowd, with the praise still ringing, he looked at the city. And he did something no one around him expected on a day of celebration.

In the King James Bible: "And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it." The Greek word is not quiet tears. When Jesus stands at Lazarus's tomb in John's Gospel, the word is a gentler one, he shed tears. Here, Luke uses the word for weeping aloud, sobbing. In the middle of the parade. And then he speaks to the city as if it were a person he loves: "If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes." Tradition hears the word for peace, shalom, in Jerusalem's name. The city of peace, and it doesn't know the things that make for peace. He goes on to describe enemies surrounding it, and walls thrown down, "because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation." A visitation is God coming close. Later, Roman armies did besiege Jerusalem and destroy the temple, and some Christians read these words as Jesus foreseeing it. But notice what he does with what he sees. He doesn't gloat or threaten. He weeps. It's grief, the way a parent grieves a child walking toward danger. The weeping and the action go together, too. He goes straight into the temple and drives out the sellers: "My house is the house of prayer." Then he teaches there daily. The leaders look for a way to destroy him, Luke says, but they can't, because "all the people were very attentive to hear him." Tears, then a cleansing, then teaching. Love for a city does all three.
screen: then, large: `IF THOU HADST KNOWN, EVEN THOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a city in conflict in mind. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a city where there's fighting or deep division right now, near or far. It could be in the news, or it could be your own town, split down the middle. Picture it from a hillside, the way Jesus saw Jerusalem: the rooftops, the streets, the ordinary people inside. Let yourself feel something for them, even grief. If you pray, you can use the psalm's words: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee, and then, in your own words, ask for peace in the city you're picturing. If you don't, hold the city in your mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Visitation. The moment weeping Jesus says Jerusalem failed to know, when God came close to the city and it didn't recognize him.
Your line: if only you knew. Today, when you read news of a place at war, stop for one breath and let yourself care before you scroll on. Day five hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: On the Mount of Olives, the small church of Dominus Flevit, Latin for the Lord wept, marks the traditional spot, and Christians around the world pray for the peace of Jerusalem and of cities in conflict, often using the words of Psalm 122.

original.note: Greek: he wept aloud, he sobbed. stronger than John's word for Jesus' tears at Lazarus's tomb.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was sad that people didn't believe him.
what it means: in the middle of celebration, he grieves aloud for the city he loves, then cleanses its temple and teaches there.
what a scholar hears: Luke's verb is klaiō, loud weeping, not John's quiet dakryō, and the city of peace doesn't know the things of peace.

notes: ἔκλαυσεν (κλαίω, Luke 19:41) vs ἐδάκρυσεν (δακρύω, John 11:35): standard observation. Confirm.
Jerusalem's name 'long heard as related to peace (shalom)': folk and traditional etymology; the true origin is debated. Hedged; confirm.

AD 70 destruction by Rome: stated as history; the reading of 19:43–44 as foreseeing it is attributed to 'many Christians', framed as grief, not punishment. Please check tone carefully. Reviewer: many critical scholars date Luke after 70 and read 19:43–44 in that light; the script does not take a side, which seems right, but confirm. Also confirm the practice (Jerusalem as the model, then 'a city in conflict') reads as care for all its people and not as a political stance.
Dominus Flevit (1955, teardrop-shaped, Antonio Barluzzi): howItsDone mentions only the name and location. Confirm.
Practice invites saying Psalm 122:6 as written ('if you pray'), then praying in one's own words for another city; no new prayer text is supplied.

Editor review (y2 557–574 pass): the practice heading told the listener to "pray for a city in conflict"; it now invites them to hold one in mind (prayer stays optional). Cut the superlative "one of the great views on earth"; the Jerusalem/shalom link is now "tradition hears"; the uncited "about forty years later, in the year 70" became "later", and "many Christians" became "some Christians".
